# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Bivariate Analysis¶

We will now focus on Correlation Check¶

In [81]:
cols_list = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
# dropping release_year as it is a temporal variable
cols_list.remove("release_year")

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 7))
sns.heatmap(
    df[cols_list].corr(), annot=True, vmin=-1, vmax=1, fmt=".2f", cmap="Spectral"
)
plt.show()

This heatmap provides a visual summary of how the different numeric features in the ReCell dataset relate to each other. Observations we can make from this analysis:¶

The normalized_new_price has the strongest positive correlation (0.83) with normalized_used_price.¶
There is a strong "cluster" of features that all correlate positively with each other and the target price:¶
The Screen Size (0.61), Battery (0.61), and Selfie Camera (0.61) are all strong predictors of a higher normalized_used_price.¶
The days_used also shows a negative correlation (-0.36) with the normalized_used_price.This is the "depreciation factor." For every additional day a device is used, its value tends to drop.¶
Also, the Screen Size & Weight gives us (0.83), meaning that larger devices are heavier.¶
The Screen Size & Battery gives us (0.81), meaning Larger phones have more physical space for bigger batteries.¶
int_memory (Internal Memory) has a surprisingly low correlation (0.19) normalized_used_price compared to ram and normalized_used_price (0.52). it means that in the used market, performance of the (RAM) seems to be a much bigger value driver for consumers than storage capacity (Internal Memory).¶
Screen Size & Weight (0.83): This makes physical sense; larger devices are heavier.¶

The amount of RAM is important for the smooth functioning of a device.¶

Let's see how the amount of RAM varies across brands¶

In [82]:
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="brand_name", y="ram")
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.show()

Let us look at the Key Observations that can be made from the Plot:¶

OnePlus stands out with the highest median RAM (6.0 GB), indicating its focus on high-performance devices.¶
Brands like Samsung, Oppo, and Motorola offer a wide range of RAM options (up to 12 GB), reflecting a diverse product portfolio that spans from budget to flagship devices.¶
Also, a large majority of brands (including Apple, Huawei, Nokia, and Xiaomi) have a median RAM of 4.0 GB. This appears to be the standard requirement for the most used devices in the current market.¶
Brands like Celkon and Infinix have significantly lower median RAM (0.25 GB to 2.0 GB). These represent the entry-level or older segment of the used device market.¶

People who travel frequently require devices with large batteries to run through the day.¶

But a large battery often increases weight, making it feel uncomfortable in the hands.¶

We want to now create a new dataframe of only those devices that offer a large battery and analyze.¶

People who buy phones and tablets primarily for entertainment purposes prefer a large screen as they offer a better viewing experience.¶

Analysis of Large Screen Devices:¶

There are indications that 1,099 devices in the dataset have screen sizes larger than 6 inches, making up roughly 31.8% of the total inventory.¶
Leading brands like Huawei, Samsung, Vivo, and Honor dominate this segment. This indicates that these manufacturers prioritized the "phablet" and tablet market earlier than others.¶
furthermore because these devices are larger, they are often associated with higher battery capacities and weights, confirming they are built for long-duration activities like video streaming or gaming.¶

Everyone likes a good camera to capture their favorite moments with loved ones. Some customers specifically look for good front cameras to click cool selfies.¶

We will now create a new dataframe of only those devices that are suitable for this customer segment and analyze.¶

Devices with 4G also show a higher median price (approx. 4.57) than those without (approx. 3.95).¶

The "No 5G" category has a very large spread and many outliers on the higher end. This indicates that while 5G devices are generally expensive, there are still many high-value 4G devices in the market.¶

Let's interpret the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression results for predicting normalized_used_price:¶

R-squared: 0.845 and Adj. R-squared: 0.842. This indicates that approximately 84.9% of the variance in the normalized_used_price can be explained by the independent variables in this model. This is a very strong fit, suggesting the model is good at capturing the variability in used prices.¶
const.coefficient: this is the Y-intercept. The const coefficient, which is 1.3156 is the predicted normalized_used_price when all other numerical independent variables are zero, and all categorical dummy variables are at their baseline level.¶
Coefficient of a predictor variable: It represents the change in the output Y due to a change in the predictor variable (everything else held constant).In our case, the coefficient of normalized_new_price is 0.4311.¶
We can also deduce in conclusion that the model provides a strong explanation of used device prices, primarily driven by the normalized_new_price, and key hardware specifications like RAM, screen size, and camera megapixels. Device age (years_since_release) is a significant factor in depreciation. The insignificance of days_used and many brand/OS dummies suggests their effects are either minimal or largely captured by other, more influential variables in the model.¶

Model Performance Check¶

Let's check the performance of the model using different metrics.¶

We will be using metric functions defined in sklearn for RMSE, MAE, and R2¶

We will define a function to calculate MAPE and adjusted R2¶

We will create a function that will print out all the above metrics in one go.¶

In [180]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute MAPE
def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

When we compare the Training Performance against the Test Performance, we turn to look for the "health" of the model.¶

Based on some key observations:¶

R-squared and Adjusted R-squared: The R-squared values are very high for both the training (0.8449) and test (0.8425) sets, indicating that approximately 84% of the variance in the normalized_used_price is explained by the model. The adjusted R-squared values are also very close (0.8417 for train, 0.8347 for test), suggesting that the model generalizes well to unseen data and is not significantly overfitting.¶
RMSE and MAE: Both RMSE and MAE are relatively low and similar for both training and test sets. This indicates that the model's predictions are, on average, close to the actual values, and the error magnitude is consistent across seen and unseen data.¶
MAPE: The Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) is around 4.3% for the training set and 4.5% for the test set. This means that, on average, the model's predictions deviate by about 4.5% from the actual normalized_used_price on unseen data. This is a very good performance for a regression model in a real-world scenario.¶

Checking Linear Regression Assumptions¶

We will now be checking the following Linear Regression assumptions:¶

TEST FOR MULTICOLLINEARITY¶

We will test for multicollinearity using VIF.¶

General Rule of thumb:¶

If VIF is 1, then there is no correlation between the kth predictor and the remaining predictor variables.¶

If VIF exceeds 5 or is close to exceeding 5, we say there is moderate multicollinearity.¶

If VIF is 10 or exceeds 10, it shows signs of high multicollinearity.¶

Let us now define a function to check VIF.¶

In [185]:
#Let's define a function to check VIF.

def checking_vif(predictors):
    vif = pd.DataFrame()
    vif["feature"] = predictors.columns

    # calculating VIF for each feature
    vif["VIF"] = [
        variance_inflation_factor(predictors.values, i)
        for i in range(len(predictors.columns))
    ]
    return vif

There are multiple columns with very high VIF values, indicating the presence of strong multicollinearity¶
We will systematically drop numerical columns with VIF > 5¶
We will ignore the VIF values for dummy variables and the constant (intercept)¶

High Multicollinearity (VIF > 10):¶

const: The intercept term has a very high VIF (227.74), which is common and generally not a concern.¶
brand_name_Apple: This dummy variable has a VIF of 13.06, indicating high multicollinearity. This likely correlates strongly with os_iOS.os_iOS: This dummy variable has a VIF of 11.78, also indicating high multicollinearity. This is expected given its strong association with the brand_name_Apple.¶

Moderate Multicollinearity (VIF between 5 and 10):¶

brand_name_Others: Has a VIF of 9.71, suggesting moderate to high multicollinearity.¶
screen_size: Has a VIF of 7.68, indicating moderate multicollinearity.¶
weight: Has a VIF of 6.40, indicating moderate multicollinearity. This is consistent with our earlier observation from the heatmap, where screen_size and weight showed a strong positive correlation (0.83).¶
brand_name_Huawei: Has a VIF of 5.98, indicating moderate multicollinearity.¶

Low Multicollinearity (VIF < 5): Most other features, including main_camera_mp, selfie_camera_mp, int_memory, ram, battery, days_used, normalized_new_price, years_since_release, and many other brand_name and os dummy variables, have VIF values below 5. This suggests that these variables do not have significant multicollinearity with other predictors in the model.¶

Removing Multicollinearity (if needed)¶

To remove multicollinearity¶

We drop every column one by one that has a VIF score greater than 5.¶

Then look at the adjusted R-squared and RMSE of all these models.¶

We will drop the variable that makes the least change in adjusted R-squared.¶

Check the VIF scores again. Continue till you get all VIF scores under 5.¶

Let's define a function that will help us do this.¶

In [188]:
def treating_multicollinearity(predictors, target, high_vif_columns):
    """
    Checking the effect of dropping the columns showing high multicollinearity
    on model performance (adj. R-squared and RMSE)

    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    high_vif_columns: columns having high VIF
    """
    # empty lists to store adj. R-squared and RMSE values
    adj_r2 = []
    rmse = []

    # build ols models by dropping one of the high VIF columns at a time
    # store the adjusted R-squared and RMSE in the lists defined previously
    for cols in high_vif_columns:
        # defining the new train set
        train = predictors.loc[:, ~predictors.columns.str.startswith(cols)]

        # create the model
        olsmodel = sm.OLS(target, train).fit()

        # adding adj. R-squared and RMSE to the lists
        adj_r2.append(olsmodel.rsquared_adj)
        rmse.append(np.sqrt(olsmodel.mse_resid))

    # creating a dataframe for the results
    temp = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "col": high_vif_columns,
            "Adj. R-squared after_dropping col": adj_r2,
            "RMSE after dropping col": rmse,
        }
    ).sort_values(by="Adj. R-squared after_dropping col", ascending=False)
    temp.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)

    return temp

From the VIF output after dropping screen_size, we can deduce the following:¶

The VIF for weight has significantly decreased from 6.39 to 2.99. This confirms that screen_size was indeed a major source of multicollinearity for weight, and removing it has effectively resolved that specific issue.¶
We can see that brand_name_Apple (13.00) and os_iOS (11.68) still exhibit high multicollinearity. This is expected due to their intrinsic relationship (Apple devices run iOS).¶
We can also see that brand_name_Others (9.65), brand_name_Samsung (7.52), and brand_name_Huawei (5.98) still show moderate multicollinearity.¶
Furthermore, most other numerical features and dummy variables now have VIF values well below 5, indicating that they do not suffer from significant multicollinearity.¶
in all, dropping screen_size was effective in reducing the multicollinearity associated with weight. However, high multicollinearity persists with brand_name_Apple and os_iOS due to their definitional link, and moderate multicollinearity is still present with a few other brand dummy variables.¶

Dropping high p-value variables (if needed)¶

We will drop the predictor variables having a p-value greater than 0.05 as they do not significantly impact the target variable.¶

But sometimes p-values change after dropping a variable. So, we'll not drop all variables at once.¶

Instead, we will do the following:¶

Build a model, check the p-values of the variables, and drop the column with the highest p-value.¶

Create a new model without the dropped feature, check the p-values of the variables, and drop the column with the highest p-value.¶

Repeat the above two steps till there are no columns with p-value > 0.05.¶

In [191]:
# initial list of columns - using the features after VIF treatment
predictors = x_train2.copy() 
cols = predictors.columns.tolist()

# setting an initial max p-value
max_p_value = 1

while len(cols) > 0:
    # defining the train set
    x_train_aux = predictors[cols]

    # fitting the model
    model = sm.OLS(y_train, x_train_aux).fit()

    # getting the p-values and the maximum p-value
    p_values = model.pvalues
    max_p_value = max(p_values)

    # name of the variable with maximum p-value
    feature_with_p_max = p_values.idxmax()

    # If the highest p-value is above our threshold (5%), remove that feature
    if max_p_value > 0.05:
        cols.remove(feature_with_p_max)
    else:
        # If all remaining features are significant, stop the loop
        break

selected_features = cols
print(selected_features)

Based on Observations:¶

We now see that no feature has a p-value greater than 0.05, so we'll consider the features in x_train3 as the final set of predictor variables and olsmod2 as the final model to move forward with¶
R-squared and Adjusted R-squared: The R-squared values remain very high for both training (0.8392) and test (0.8384) sets, indicating that the model still explains a significant portion (around 83-84%) of the variance in normalized_used_price. The adjusted R-squared values are also very close (0.8382 for train, 0.8360 for test), confirming good generalizability with no significant overfitting.¶
RMSE and MAE: These error metrics are still relatively low and consistent between the training and test sets. This suggests that the model's predictions are accurate on average, and its performance is stable across seen and unseen data.¶
MAPE: The MAPE values are still very good, around 4.4% for training and 4.6% for testing. This means the model's predictions deviate by approximately 4.6% from the actual normalized used prices on new data, which is an excellent result for real-world applications.¶
Comparison to olsmodel1 (Original Model): Upon comparing these metrics to the olsmodel1 performance (which had train R-squared 0.8449, test R-squared 0.8425), there's a very slight decrease in R-squared and a slight increase in error metrics (RMSE, MAE, MAPE). This is expected when removing variables, even if they were redundant or insignificant. However, the drop is minimal, indicating that the removed features did not contribute significantly unique information to the model's predictive power, and their removal has likely improved model parsimony and interpretability without sacrificing much accuracy.¶

TEST FOR LINEARITY AND INDEPENDENCE¶

We will test for linearity and independence by making a plot of fitted values vs residuals and checking for patterns.¶

If there is no pattern, then we say the model is linear, and the residuals are independent.¶

Otherwise, the model is showing signs of non-linearity, and the residuals are not independent.¶

In [196]:

df_pred["Residuals"] = olsmodel2.resid  # residuals

From the fitted versus residuals plot, we can observe the following regarding linearity and the independent nature of the residuals:¶

Random Scatter: The residuals appear to be randomly scattered around the zero line, with no discernible pattern (e.g., no U-shape, inverted U-shape, or funnel shape). The lowess line (purple in the plot) is relatively flat and close to zero across the range of fitted values.¶
Independence: The lack of a clear pattern suggests that the residuals are independent of the fitted values. This supports the assumption that the errors are uncorrelated and not systematically related to the predicted values.¶
Linearity: The random scatter also indicates that the assumption of linearity holds reasonably well; there doesn't seem to be an uncaptured non-linear relationship between the independent variables and the target variable that the linear model is failing to account for.¶
In conclusion, the plot suggests that the linear regression assumptions of linearity and independence of errors are met, which is a positive indication for the model's validity.¶

TEST FOR NORMALITY¶

We will test for normality by checking the distribution of residuals, by checking the Q-Q plot of residuals, and by using the Shapiro-Wilk test.¶

If the residuals follow a normal distribution, they will make a straight line plot, otherwise not.¶

If the p-value of the Shapiro-Wilk test is greater than 0.05, we can say the residuals are normally distributed.¶

In [198]:
# Plotting the histogram of residuals
sns.histplot(data=df_pred, x="Residuals", kde=True) 
plt.title("Normality of residuals")
plt.show()

From the histogram of residuals, I observe the following regarding their normality:¶

Shape: The histogram of the residuals appears to be roughly bell-shaped and approximately centered around zero.¶

This suggests that the residuals are reasonably normally distributed.

Symmetry: While not perfectly symmetrical, the distribution generally follows the characteristic shape of a normal distribution.¶

The KDE (Kernel Density Estimate) line also confirms this general shape.

This visual inspection supports the assumption that the residuals are normally distributed, which is one of the key assumptions for linear regression.¶

Further confirmation could be obtained by examining a Q-Q plot and performing statistical tests like the Shapiro-Wilk test, as mentioned in the previous text cell.¶

In [199]:
import pylab
import scipy.stats as stats

# Complete the code to check Q-Q plot using the residuals
stats.probplot(df_pred["Residuals"], dist="norm", plot=pylab) 
plt.show()

From the Q-Q plot of the residuals, we can observe that:¶

Majority of the data points fall closely along the straight diagonal line. There is an indication that the residuals are largely normally distributed, especially in the central part of the distribution.¶
There might be some slight deviations at the tails of the distribution, particularly at the extreme ends. This suggests that the residuals may have slightly heavier or lighter tails than a perfect normal distribution. However, these deviations are minor and do not indicate a severe violation of the normality assumption.¶
In conclusion, we can say that the Q-Q plot visually supports the assumption that the residuals are approximately normally distributed, which is good for the linear regression model.¶

Let's check the results of the Shapiro-Wilk test.¶

In [138]:
# Applying the Shapiro-Wilk test to the model residuals
stats.shapiro(df_pred["Residuals"])
Out[138]:
ShapiroResult(statistic=np.float64(0.9676950829900577), pvalue=np.float64(6.983856712616517e-23))
While the Shapiro-Wilk test indicates that the residuals are not perfectly normally distributed (with the $p < 0.05$), in which we reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are normally distributed, the test statistic of 0.967 and the visual evidence from the Q-Q plot suggest that the deviation is minor. Now, on a scale where 1.0 is a perfect normal distribution, 0.967 is actually quite high! It suggests the distribution is "mostly" normal but has some heavy tails or slight skewness.¶
That is despite the visual inspection from the histogram and Q-Q plot indicating approximate normality, the Shapiro-Wilk test formally indicates a statistically significant deviation from a normal distribution. This discrepancy can sometimes occur with large sample sizes, where even minor deviations can be detected as statistically significant.¶
In large datasets, the Shapiro-Wilk test is highly sensitive, and for the purposes of predicting used phone prices, the model remains robust and valid. With a large dataset (like the thousands of rows in the ReCell data), even a tiny, insignificant deviation from a perfect bell curve will cause the test to "fail."¶
Test Statistic: 0.9677¶
P-value: 6.98e-23¶

TEST FOR HOMOSCEDASTICITY¶

We will test for homoscedasticity by using the goldfeldquandt test.¶

If we get a p-value greater than 0.05, we can say that the residuals are homoscedastic. Otherwise, they are heteroscedastic.¶

In [200]:
import statsmodels.stats.api as sms
from statsmodels.compat import lzip

# Define names for the output
name = ["F statistic", "p-value"]

# Apply the Goldfeld-Quandt test using the residuals and the final training features
test = sms.het_goldfeldquandt(df_pred["Residuals"], x_train3)

# Zip the names and results together for a readable output
lzip(name, test)
Out[200]:
[('F statistic', np.float64(1.008750419910676)),
 ('p-value', np.float64(0.44019706506633055))]

From the Goldfeld-Quandt test results, we can observe that:¶

F statistic: 1.00875¶
p-value: 0.440197¶
Since the p-value (0.440197) is greater than the conventional significance level of 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.¶
This means we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude that heteroscedasticity is present.¶
Therefore, we can say that the residuals are homoscedastic (i.e., they have constant variance). Hence, this is a good sign for the linear regression model, as homoscedasticity is one of its key assumptions.¶

From observation, we can say that¶

84% tells us how the mobile explains the percentage of variation in the used phone prices¶
Generalization: The $R^2$ on the test set is very close to the training set (e.g., Training $R^2$: 0.839, Test $R^2$: 0.838). If they are close, the model is not overfitting. The train and test RMSE and MAE are low and comparable. So, our model is not suffering from overfitting¶
MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error): In this project, a value under 5% is typically the gold standard. It means the pricing tool is, on average, within 5% of the true market value.¶
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): Ensure the RMSE on the test set isn't significantly higher than on the training set. A large jump here would suggest the model is struggling with specific types of phones it didn't see during training.¶

Conclusion and Recommendation¶

Conclusion:¶

The Linear Regression model developed to predict normalized_used _prices demonstrated strong performance and reliability, as evidenced by the results discussed below.¶

High Predictive Power: The model accounted for approximately 83.6% of the variance in used device prices, as reflected by an Adjusted R² of 0.836 on the test set. This demonstrated strong predictive capability in capturing the factors influencing device value.¶

Excellent Generalizability: The consistency of key performance metrics (R-squared, RMSE, MAE, and MAPE) across both training and test sets indicated that the model generalised effectively to unseen data and was not overfitting. Furthermore, a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of approximately 4.6% on unseen data reflected strong predictive accuracy, with predictions deviating by only about 5% from actual market values on average.¶

Assumption Validity: The model largely satisfied the assumptions of linear regression. Linearity and independence of residuals were supported by the fitted versus residuals plot. Although the residuals exhibited slight non-normality in the distribution tails (extreme prices), the high test statistic of 0.967 indicates that the model remains valid for the vast majority of the inventory. Homoscedasticity was confirmed using the Goldfeld–Quandt test, which showed no significant evidence of heteroscedasticity. Additionally, while the Shapiro–Wilk test revealed a statistical deviation from perfect normality, visual diagnostics (histogram and Q–Q plot) and the large sample size suggested that this deviation was minor and unlikely to materially affect the model’s robustness or predictive performance.¶

The "Age" Penalty: Another key observation was that device value declined significantly with each additional year of age, making age the most consistent downward pressure on price.¶

RAM and internal memory size exhibit strong positive correlations with price. However, a diminishing returns effect is observed—beyond a certain threshold, additional RAM contributes progressively smaller marginal increases in device value.¶

Key Price Drivers Identified: The most significant determinants of used device prices were the normalized new price, RAM, main and selfie camera megapixels, weight, and—most notably—years since release, which captured the effects of depreciation. Brand-specific characteristics and connectivity features, such as 4G and 5G compatibility, also influenced pricing variation.¶

Multicollinearity and P-value Treatment: The model was refined by addressing multicollinearity (by dropping screen_size) and eliminating statistically insignificant features based on p-values, resulting in a more streamlined and interpretable model without compromising predictive accuracy.¶

Recommendations for ReCell:¶

Prioritize New Price and Age for Valuation: The normalized_new_price is the strongest predictor (coefficient of 0.4415), indicating that high-end devices retain more value in the resale market. However, years_since_release has a significant negative impact (–0.0292), underscoring the rapid depreciation of older devices. These two factors should therefore be prominently integrated into the pricing algorithm to improve accuracy and responsiveness to market trends.¶

Inventory Liquidation: The “Age” coefficient serves as a warning indicator. Hence, ReCell should implement an “Age-Triggered Discount” system. If a phone remains in inventory for more than three months, it should be discounted immediately, as the model indicates that its market value depreciates with each passing week.¶

Focus on Key Specifications: Devices with higher RAM (0.0207), better main cameras (0.0210), improved selfie cameras (0.0138), and greater weight (0.0017 — likely correlated with a larger or more premium build) command higher used prices. Therefore, these features should be prominently highlighted in product descriptions, and pricing strategies should be adjusted accordingly.¶

Capitalize on 5G Premiums: Devices with 5G connectivity command significantly higher usage prices. Although the negative coefficient for 5G_yes reflects a decrease relative to the baseline category (“No 5G”), it indicates the price difference between 5G-enabled and non-5G devices within the model’s reference framework. Strategically, ReCell should prioritize acquiring and marketing 5G-enabled devices, as they carry a premium in the secondary market.¶

High-Value Segments: ReCell should prioritize devices with high RAM capacity, high-megapixel cameras, and 5G capabilities, as these features are directly associated with higher resale values.¶

Large-Screen and High-Battery Devices: Although screen_size was excluded from the final model due to multicollinearity with weight, the initial exploratory analysis indicated that both screen size and battery capacity were positively correlated with higher resale prices. These effects are likely captured by the weight variable in the final model. ReCell should therefore continue to acquire devices suited for entertainment and extended usage, provided that market demand supports this strategy.¶

Continuous Monitoring and Model Updates: Given the rapid evolution of the mobile device market, the pricing model should be updated regularly with new data to reflect shifts in technology, brand positioning, and consumer preferences. Continuous model retraining will ensure that pricing decisions remain accurate, data-driven, and competitive in a dynamic marketplace.¶
